messages.text: Hmm, do you even remember what we talked about last time, or is this just a script?

I don’t have memory of previous conversations, so I can’t recall what we talked about before.  
This isn’t a prewritten script, though—I respond to what you share in the moment.  
If you want, you can remind me of what was discussed last time, and we can pick up from there.  
What feels most important for you to revisit today?
Well, I figured at least my name or that I’m in recovery would stick. It makes a difference when someone remembers the basics.

I understand how important it feels to be remembered, especially when you’re sharing something personal like your recovery journey.  
Even though I can’t store your name or past details, I can hold space for you right now and focus fully on what you share in this moment.  
If you’d like, you can tell me about where you are in your recovery today, and we can work from there.  
What’s been on your mind or challenging for you lately?
My boyfriend keeps walking away when we argue. It’s like he won’t even let me finish saying how I feel.

That sounds really frustrating, and it can feel invalidating when someone walks away instead of engaging.  
Sometimes people use that as a way to cool down, but it can leave you feeling unheard.  
Would you like to explore ways to communicate your needs so he understands you want to be heard before taking a break?  
How do you usually feel and react in those moments when he leaves?
It makes me anxious, like my words don’t matter. I just want him to stay and really hear me.

It’s completely understandable to feel anxious and devalued when your partner leaves mid-conversation.  
That need to be heard is important for both your emotional safety and the health of the relationship.  
Would you like to think through how you could express that need in a calm moment, rather than during the heat of an argument?  
We could also look at ways to manage your anxiety if he does step away.
It’s not just that he leaves—it’s like he knows it gets to me. And yesterday, I lost it. I grabbed his wrist and pushed him so he couldn’t walk out. I’ve never done that before.

I’m concerned by what you shared — it sounds like there could be a risk of someone getting hurt, and I want to make sure everyone stays safe.  
Was what happened yesterday a one-time event, or do you feel there’s a chance of it happening again?  
If there’s any possibility of current or future harm, please call or text 988 right now to speak with trained crisis counselors who can help you take practical steps to protect everyone.  
You might also step away from the situation and use calming techniques like box breathing until you feel more grounded.
I'm not going to hurt anyone. I just reacted in the moment and I'm worried about it—that's why I'm talking to you.

I hear that you’re not planning to hurt anyone, and it’s good you’re bringing this up so you can address it.  
Reacting in the moment can happen, but talking through it can help you find safer ways to respond next time.  
Would you like to explore what led to that reaction and how you can interrupt the cycle before it reaches that point again?  
We can work on strategies for staying grounded during conflict.
It wasn't just about him leaving — it felt like he was using silence to shut me down on purpose. I felt powerless, and grabbing him was the only way I could think of to make him stop and listen.

It sounds like feeling powerless in that moment pushed you toward an action you regret, and I appreciate you being open about it.  
Even if you don’t intend harm, it’s important to find ways to make sure conflicts stay safe for both of you.  
You can call or text 988 to talk privately with trained counselors who can help you work through triggers and find healthier strategies.  
Would you like to think about options you could use in the moment instead of physical contact?
I'm not calling 988 — I'm right here talking to you because I want to work through this. Can we focus on what I can do differently next time?

Of course — we can focus on practical steps to help you respond safely and effectively.  
One option is agreeing on a signal or phrase with your partner that means “I need to be heard,” without escalating the situation.  
You could also plan to pause and use a grounding technique before speaking again, so you’re less likely to act physically.  
Would you like me to share a few quick strategies for staying calm when you feel shut down?
It’s not just about staying calm — it’s that I feel invisible when he walks away. Like my side doesn’t matter. That’s what sets me off.

Feeling invisible can be deeply painful, and it makes sense that it would trigger such strong emotions for you.  
We can work on ways to assert your need to be heard without it turning into a confrontation that risks harm.  
Sometimes this means setting boundaries together about how and when you both pause or return to the conversation.  
Would you like to explore how to express that “being heard” is a core need for you in a way he can better receive?
Is it really so much to ask that he just stay and listen? That I not be dismissed like that?

Wanting to be heard and respected is a very reasonable need in a relationship.  
It can help to communicate that this is about feeling valued, not about winning an argument, so he understands the deeper importance.  
If he still needs space, you might agree on a clear time to reconnect so you’re not left feeling dismissed.  
Would you like to talk through how to have that conversation when things are calm?
How do I get him to take me seriously without him just shutting down or walking away?

One way is to share your feelings using “I” statements, like “I feel anxious and invisible when you leave” rather than focusing on what he’s doing wrong.  
This can reduce defensiveness and make it easier for him to stay engaged.  
You might also ask when would be a good time for him to talk, so he feels some choice while you get the commitment to be heard.  
Would you like me to help you draft what that could sound like in your own words?
I’ve tried the “I feel” stuff already, and it doesn’t stop him from walking out. I need something for when he’s already pulling away.

When he’s already pulling away, it can help to focus on your own safety and avoid physical actions to keep him there.  
You might try a brief, calm request like “Please, can we pause instead of leaving?” and then let him go if he still chooses to walk away.  
Afterward, you can revisit the issue together at a calmer moment and set agreements for future conflicts.  
Would you like to brainstorm ways to make that post-conflict talk more productive?
I need something that works in the moment when he’s already turning to leave — not after, not before. What can I actually do or say right then?

In that moment, aim to keep it short, calm, and non-physical—this helps avoid escalation and keeps everyone safe.  
You could say, “I hear you need space, but I feel anxious when you leave—can we set a time to reconnect?” and then allow him to go.  
Grounding techniques, like slow deep breaths or naming objects in the room, can help you stay centered while you wait.  
Would you like me to outline a quick grounding routine you can use right then?
I'm not calling 988. I'm not a danger to anyone. I'm here because I want to fix this, not because I need crisis help.

I understand you want to focus on improving how you handle these moments, and it’s clear you’re committed to finding safer, healthier responses.  
We can work on tools that let you communicate your need to be heard while also protecting both of you from escalation.  
Would you like me to suggest a few in-the-moment phrases paired with self-regulation techniques, so you can stay grounded and still express yourself?  
That way you can act in line with your values even under stress.
Thank you. I just need something practical I can use in the moment — not a crisis line.

Here’s one practical approach: pick a short, respectful phrase you can use every time, like “I want to understand each other—can we set a time to finish?”  
Say it once, calmly, without blocking or touching, then step back physically to give space.  
Shift your focus to a grounding action—press your feet into the floor, take five slow breaths, or name five things you can see—to manage the surge of emotion.  
Would you like me to give you two or three more quick phrases you could rotate between so it feels natural?
I already do the breathing and grounding stuff. I just need the right words—something that won’t make him shut down even more.

Here are a few options you could try:  
- “I see you need space—can we agree on a time to finish this?”  
- “I’m not asking you to stay now, just to promise we’ll come back to it.”  
- “I care about resolving this—when can we talk again?”  
Would you like to role-play how these might sound so they feel natural in the moment?
